topics: KMS vs HSM, key rotation, signed audit bundles
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE. Samir our SE will co‑lead. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Elena Rossi: Elena here, Head of Infra at Novara. Priya and Tomás here as well.
[00:12] Priya Nair: Hey all.
[00:14] Tomás Alvarez: Tomás, GRC.
[00:16] Maya Chen: Great. Quick agenda: control plane isolation, ingress/egress patterns, identity + RBAC, KMS/HSM questions, and audit logs. Any additions?
[00:24] Elena Rossi: No, that's it. We're mainly concerned about being able to show auditors a clean chain for key rotation and prove no egress to third-party data centers.
[00:33] Samir Patel: Hey, quick note — our private deploy ships a control plane that can be colocated in customer VPC or run as a customer‑managed control plane. We also support an airgapped mode for highly regulated customers.
[00:43] Priya Nair: When you say airgapped mode, is the control plane fully offline? How do we get audit logs out? We have to give auditors signed bundles, not a live stream.
[00:52] Samir Patel: Right. The airgap option allows the control plane to run with no outbound internet egress. Audit logs are exported as signed bundles — think gzipped JSON with an HSM signature — which you can physically transfer or SCP to your audit archive. We do local signing when an HSM is attached, otherwise we sign with a customer KMS key.
[01:10] Tomás Alvarez: Is HSM FIPS 140-2 level? We need attestations for ISO and a note on algorithm suites.
[01:18] Samir Patel: We support AWS CloudHSM and external PKCS#11 HSMs. The attestation includes algorithm enumerations (RSA/ECDSA), key IDs, and rotation timestamps. We can provide a sample attestation PDF.
[01:28] Elena Rossi: Good. Next, network segmentation: we run a strict egress proxy model and we want to ensure nothing from the inference pods can call out except through that egress gateway. How does Redwood recommend enforcing that?
[01:39] Samir Patel: Common approach: 1) strict VPC subnet segmentation, 2) pod-level egress via eBPF or iptables rules, 3) enforce service mesh mTLS so only sidecars can talk to the egress gateway, and 4) deny all outbound by default with explicit allowlist for needed destinations (artifact buckets, KMS endpoints, telemetry collectors).
[01:58] Priya Nair: We don't want telemetry to go out to Redwood's hosted backend. Telemetry must be to our SIEM. Is that possible?
[02:05] Maya Chen: Yes — Redwood Private can push logs/metrics to your collectors (Syslog/FluentD/OTLP). We support disabling remote telemetry to Redwood and keeping everything inside your VPC. The only exception is optional -- if you need Redwood support, you can stream redacted snippets via a support bridge.
[02:22] Elena Rossi: Ok. Can you walk through typical firewall/NACL setup?
[02:26] Samir Patel: Sure. High level: control plane subnets are segregated from worker subnets. Control plane egress is blocked by default. Management access goes through a bastion in a management subnet — jumpbox with SAML-backed ephemeral credentials. Workers only egress to the egress gateway IPs via enforced network policies. For egress to KMS endpoints, use VPC endpoints or PrivateLink wherever possible.
[02:48] Priya Nair: Does Redwood require any public IPs on worker nodes?
[02:52] Samir Patel: No. We recommend private-only workers. Public IPs are only used for management bastions when necessary and are optional.
[02:58] Tomás Alvarez: On RBAC: we use Okta and SAML. We also have strict separation between infra ops and app owners. How granular is Redwood's RBAC?
[03:08] Maya Chen: We integrate with SAML/Okta for SSO and SCIM for provisioning. RBAC is role- and resource-based: you can create roles scoped to model routes, deployment environments, and audit view-only roles. We also support fine-grained temporary elevation for break-glass — auditable and tied to an approval workflow.
[03:26] Priya Nair: Can we hook to our existing approval workflow (ServiceNow)?
[03:29] Samir Patel: Yes, via webhook connectors. We can emit an approval request and record its outcome in the audit log.
[03:35] Elena Rossi: About audit logs: our auditors want immutable logs, with proof of non-repudiation. How do you handle tamper evidence?
[03:43] Samir Patel: Logs are written to append-only stores, optionally to your S3 buckets with Object Lock (WORM). For non-repudiation we provide signed audit bundles, timestamped and HSM-signed. Bundle includes config diffs, key rotation events, policy changes, and user actions.
[03:58] Tomás Alvarez: If we rotate keys, is there a period where old tokens are valid? We need to tie a token's validity window to a rotation event for proof.
[04:07] Samir Patel: We expose explicit rotation events and deprecation windows. Tokens issued under an old key are trackable; the audit bundle links token IDs to key fingerprints and rotation timestamps. You can set zero-window rotation if you want immediate invalidation, but expect short-lived RPC retrys.
[04:24] Priya Nair: For encryption at rest, does Redwood re-encrypt model weights after key rotation or rely on envelope encryption?
[04:31] Samir Patel: We use envelope encryption. Master key rotation is supported, and we rotate the data-encryption keys (DEKs) lazily on access unless you opt into an eager rewrap job. We can run a one-time background rewrap for compliance windows.
[04:46] Elena Rossi: On data residency: we must ensure embeddings and logs for EU customers remain in EU. How strict is your regional routing?
[04:54] Maya Chen: We route by policy to region-bound variants. In Private mode you control placement — workers and storage are in your VPC, so residency is under your control. For hosted, we have region pinning and data locality guarantees in contract.
[05:08] Tomás Alvarez: A quick tangent: do you support signed log bundles that omit PII or can redact? Auditors sometimes need redacted output for third-party reviewers.
[05:17] Samir Patel: Yes, the bundle generator supports a redaction policy. It can either redact or mask PII fields before signing; the signing attests to the redaction version so the chain is clear.
[05:30] Elena Rossi: Great. Now, more hands‑on: can you demo the HSM key rotation flow in a lab? We want to see how an external PKCS#11 HSM integrates and how the audit bundle captures it.
[05:40] Samir Patel: We can't demo live in this call, but we can schedule a lab. I will prepare a run with CloudHSM and a simulated on‑prem PKCS#11 HSM. The flow will show: key creation, attach to instance, rotation request, active key swap, bundle export.
[05:57] Priya Nair: Please include the signed bundle format — we need to show auditors the exact fields.
[06:02] Maya Chen: We'll include a sample bundle.
[06:05] Elena Rossi: On network controls, can you show a sample iptables/eBPF rule set that prevents direct outbound to internet from pods? Our infra team wants specifics.
[06:13] Samir Patel: We'll share a minimal set. Typical policy: default DROP on OUTPUT for pod namespace, allow to kube-dns, egress-gateway CIDR, and VPC endpoint CIDRs. We also prefer using cgroup- or eBPF-based egress enforcement for performance vs iptables churn.
[06:29] Tomás Alvarez: How do you secure the egress gateway itself?
[06:32] Samir Patel: The egress gateway runs in a dedicated subnet, behind NACLs and a host firewall. We enforce mTLS and client certs between worker sidecars and the gateway. The gateway performs destination allowlist and can do TLS origination with certs stored in HSM or KMS.
[06:49] Priya Nair: Is there deep packet inspection or do you recommend only SNI/host-based enforcement?
[06:54] Samir Patel: For privacy, we avoid DPI by default. We recommend SNI and destination IP allowlists; for customers that require content inspection we can integrate with an inline DLP appliance in the egress path. That typically needs more throughput headroom.
[07:09] Elena Rossi: Let's talk about backup and disaster: if the control plane is airgapped and something corrupts, how do we bring it back? Do you support signed backup snapshots?
[07:19] Samir Patel: Yes. Snapshots are exported as signed, versioned artifacts. We recommend regular automated snapshots that are then pushed to an immutable archive. Recovery playbooks are included in the runbook we will send.
[07:31] Tomás Alvarez: On SSO provisioning, can we map Okta groups to Redwood roles and limit who can push a model? We want separation of duties.
[07:39] Maya Chen: Absolutely. SCIM group mapping to roles is supported. You can have groups for model-pushers, operators, and auditors. Auditors can be granted view-only role with access to signed bundles.
[07:49] Priya Nair: Any guidance on token lifetimes? We prefer short-lived tokens and session-based access.
[07:55] Samir Patel: We default to short-lived tokens (15m) with refresh flows. Ops can request longer service tokens bound to IPs and TTL, but those are only for automated CI/CD agents and need explicit RBAC and audit trail.
[08:08] Elena Rossi: One of our engineers asked about kernel-level exploits — can we run FIPS validated kernels and have mandatory patch windows?
[08:16] Samir Patel: You control the OS in private deployments. We publish an SRE patching cadence and can sign-off on your kernel builds. For on-prem airgapped environments we provide patch bundles you can vet and apply.
[08:27] Tomás Alvarez: What about network flow logs? We need to be able to tie outbound connection attempts to user actions. Any mapping?
[08:34] Samir Patel: We correlate flow logs with request IDs in the audit bundle. Each inference request is stamped with a trace-id; the egress gateway logs include that ID. Bundle includes correlation table.
[08:44] Priya Nair: Are there known limitations? I want to capture any gaps before audit prep.
[08:49] Samir Patel: Known caveats: if you opt for immediate rewrap of all DEKs you should expect increased I/O; DLP inline appliances add latency; airgapped support requires you to manage physical transfer of bundles. We'll document mitigations.
[09:02] Elena Rossi: Ok, let's recap and finalize next steps.
[09:06] Maya Chen: Recap — Redwood will send: SOC2/ISO control mapping, sample signed audit bundle, iptables/eBPF examples, and a proposed lab schedule for HSM demo. Novara will share egress destination list and Okta group mapping.
[09:18] Tomás Alvarez: Correct. Also note, we'll want a short written statement about key custody model for procurement.
[09:24] Maya Chen: We'll include key custody language. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with calendar invites for the lab.
[09:31] Elena Rossi: Thanks.
[09:32] Meeting Ended

Notes: transcription includes sporadic mis-hears (e.g., "key sings" -> "key signs" in auto transcript), occasional latency markers removed. Links referenced: private-deploy-runbook_v2.pdf (will be shared), signed-audit-bundle-spec.md (will be shared).
